title: Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. Federal Power Commission (1974)
shortTitle: Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. Federal Power Commission (1974)
summary: A policy statement announces a tentative position that the agency must justify when applying it, rather than supplying an already binding norm.
notes: The case concerned FPC Order No. 467 setting curtailment priorities for natural gas; the court held the order was a general statement of policy exempt from notice and comment because it did not establish a 'binding norm' and left the agency free to justify its position in later adjudications.

sections.Parties: The caption identifies Pacific Gas & Electric and the Federal Power Commission. The assigned excerpt presents the court’s general analysis of policy statements; it does not supply the participants’ specific regulatory dispute.
sections.Material Facts: The supplied passage contrasts a legislative rule, which establishes a legal standard, with an announcement of the policy the agency intends to pursue in later rulemaking or adjudication. The underlying transaction or regulatory program at issue is omitted.
sections.Procedural History: The D.C. Circuit issued the opinion in 1974.
sections.Issue: What distinguishes a general policy statement from a substantive rule carrying the force of law?
sections.Holding: The excerpt identifies the key distinction as the statement’s practical effect in later proceedings: a policy statement does not finally determine rights or create a binding norm.
sections.Reasoning: A legislative rule ordinarily fixes the underlying policy for later applications, leaving questions such as factual compliance and waiver. A policy statement instead gives advance information about a position the agency may pursue; its policy remains open to challenge. When relying on it in an individual matter, the agency must justify its position through evidence and reasoning as though it had not previously announced the statement. The court recognized the value of disclosing intentions for planning and national consistency. The following Community Nutrition discussion qualifies the simple account by examining whether the agency binds its own enforcement discretion, even without automatically establishing regulated parties’ liability.
